newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russian Duma throws out government's budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russian Duma throws out government's budget.

text.p: Russia's State Duma lower house of parliament rejected the goverment's 1997 budget on Friday but left a final decision on the fate of the bill until next week.
Deputies threw out the draft by 280 votes to 33, after representatives of every party and group in the Duma -- including government supporters -- spoke out against the plans.
"The draft is unrealistic, and revenues and expenditure are unbalanced," said Yury Maslyukov, communist chairman of the Duma's economic policy committee.

"The draft 1997 budget...does not contain adequate measures to reactivate industrial and industrial policy or social policy," added Maslyukov, who was once chairman of the former Soviet planning commission Gosplan.
The Duma agreed to set up a working group which will discuss which of two alternatives to present to deputies on Wednesday, October 16. The group will meet on Monday.
One possibility is to reject the draft outright and order the government to produce a new one within 20 days.

Alternatively, the Duma can call for the formation of a tripartite conciliation commission, with representatives from the Duma, the Federation Council upper house and the government, to thrash out the differences.

The rejected draft envisaged spending next year of 524.34 trillion roubles ($97 billion), revenof 433.64 trillion and a deficit of 90.70 trillion, or 3.3 percent of gross domestic produ Speakers for the Communist Party and its allies urged
outright rejection of the budget.
This would force the government to take full responsibility for the budget rather than involve the opposition parties.
But the pro-government Our Home is Russia party, the liberal Yabloko party and extreme nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky's Liberal Democratic Party called for a conciliation commission.
"We can't leave money up to the government alone," Zhirinovsky told deputies. "It would be like letting criminals draw up the criminal code."
Opposition deputies say the budget will not do enough to revive the recession-hit economy.
Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin acknowledged Russia was in a crisis but recent achievements such as stabilising the rouble and bringing down inflation meant it was poised for growth.
"It's possible to say that we have a situation in the economy which is favourable for growth," he said. "On the other hand the country is living through an extremely acute crisis."
Yasin forecast inflation would be 10 to 13 percent next year, and GDP would be unchanged after a five percent drop this year, if the budget proposals were accepted in full.
Otherwise inflation of 21 to 25 percent and a further fall of up to two percent in industrial output were likely, he said.
The recession has been aggravated by a tangle of debts and unpaid bills, in which the government does not receive the taxes it is due and cannot meet many of its spending commitments.
The State Tax Service said this week the government had collected only 45 percent of budgeted taxes in September while January-September collection was just 75 percent of target.
President Boris Yeltsin on Friday created a special commission to improve tax collection and said better revenue was the only way to lower tax rates.

"I know taxes are high in Russia today, but we will be able to lower them only if we manage to ensure compliance with tax legislation," said Yeltsin, who faces an operation in the next two months to improve blood supply to his heart.
Yeltsin made clear that better tax collection was the only way to raise enough money to pay off a huge backlog of wages to pensioners, servicemen and workers in the state sector.
